questions.q: A Streams application reads one topic with 10 partitions. The team runs 14 instances with one thread each. What happens?

options.t: Ten instances process data and four are idle
All 14 share the work, each taking about 0.7 of a partition
options.why: A partition's task runs on one thread; it isn't split.

options.t: Kafka Streams adds 4 partitions to the input topic
options.why: Streams never changes an input topic's partition count.

options.t: The four extra instances fail to start
options.why: They start and join, but get no tasks.

questions.explain: Parallelism is set by input partitions: with ten partitions you can run up to ten instances; further instances are idle.

questions.q: An application has 6 input partitions and runs on one instance. How can it use more CPU cores on that machine?

options.t: Raise num.stream.threads (default 1) up to 6
Raise num.standby.replicas to 6
options.why: Standbys keep state copies; they don't process records.

options.t: Set processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2
options.why: This changes guarantees, not parallelism.

options.t: Lower commit.interval.ms to 100
options.why: Committing more often doesn't add processing threads.

questions.explain: Threads run tasks; `num.stream.threads` (default 1) sets how many an instance uses. Tasks, and so useful threads in total, are bounded by the input partitions.

questions.q: An instance running a stateful task crashes, and the task moves to another instance. How does its state store get rebuilt?

options.t: From a backup that the crashed instance uploaded every hour
options.why: Kafka Streams has no such backup; it uses changelog topics.

options.t: By re-reading the input topic from the beginning
options.why: Restoration replays the changelog, not the input.

options.t: It isn't rebuilt; the task starts with empty state
options.why: Kafka Streams restores state to its content before the failure.

options.t: By replaying the store's changelog topic before processing

questions.explain: Each state store has a replicated changelog topic. A task restarted elsewhere restores its store by replaying the changelog before it resumes processing.

questions.q: After failovers, state restoration takes several minutes for a large store. Which setting is meant to shorten it?

options.t: num.standby.replicas
num.stream.threads
options.why: More threads don't make a task's restore start from a caught-up copy.

options.t: statestore.cache.max.bytes
options.why: The record cache doesn't hold a copy of the store for failover.

options.t: replication.factor
options.why: This protects the changelog topic, not restore time.

questions.explain: Standby replicas keep caught-up copies of local state on other instances, so a migrated task can be placed where a copy already exists, cutting restore time.

questions.q: What is the default persistent state store in Kafka Streams?

options.t: An in-memory hash map
options.why: In-memory stores exist, but they aren't the persistent default.

options.t: A compacted Kafka topic queried directly
options.why: Topics back stores as changelogs; queries go to the local store.

options.t: RocksDB on local disk
An external database the app connects to
options.why: Kafka Streams state is local to the application.

questions.explain: RocksDB is the default persistent store, recommended for most uses: it keeps data on local disk and can hold more than the heap.

questions.q: Which TWO statements about the internal topics a Streams application creates are right?

options.t: A key-value store's changelog topic is compacted
Repartition topics are compacted
options.why: Repartition topics use delete, with infinite retention.

options.t: Their names start with the application.id
They must be created by an administrator first
options.why: The application creates them (it needs permission to on a secured cluster).

options.t: They are shared by every Streams application
options.why: Internal topics are used only by the application that created them.

questions.explain: Internal topics are named `<application.id>-<operatorName>-<suffix>`. Key-value store changelogs are compacted; repartition topics use delete with infinite retention.

questions.q: In Kafka Streams 4.3, what happens by default when a record in an input topic can't be deserialized?

options.t: It is skipped, and a warning is written to the application log
options.why: That is LogAndContinueExceptionHandler, which you must configure.

options.t: It is sent to a dead-letter topic
options.why: Only if errors.dead.letter.queue.topic.name is set.

options.t: The processing fails, with LogAndFailExceptionHandler
It is retried until it deserializes
options.why: A record that can't be deserialized won't succeed on retry.

questions.explain: `deserialization.exception.handler` defaults to `LogAndFailExceptionHandler` (stop). `LogAndContinueExceptionHandler` skips bad records, and a dead-letter topic is used only when configured.

questions.q: A GPS reading is taken at 08:00, reaches the broker at 08:02 and is processed at 08:05. Which is its event time?

options.why: That is ingestion time, when the broker appended it.
That is processing time.

options.t: Whichever is latest
options.why: Event time is when the event happened at the source.

questions.explain: Event time is when the event happened at the source; ingestion time when the broker appended it; processing time when the application processes it.

questions.q: A processor schedules a punctuator every 10 seconds with `PunctuationType.STREAM_TIME`. No new records arrive for an hour. How often does it fire in that hour?

options.t: Every 10 seconds, 360 times
options.why: That's wall-clock punctuation.

options.t: Once, at the end of the hour
options.why: Nothing advances stream time during the hour.

options.t: Every 10 seconds of processing CPU time
options.why: Punctuation uses stream time or wall-clock time, not CPU time.

options.t: Never: stream time only advances with input

questions.explain: Stream-time punctuation is driven by data: stream time advances with the timestamps of input records, so with no new input, `punctuate()` isn't called.

questions.q: A dashboard wants to read the current count per key from a running Streams application's state store. Which statement is right?

options.t: Each instance queries its local stores; reaching others needs your own RPC layer
Kafka Streams runs a built-in REST server that serves every store of every instance
options.why: You add your own RPC layer, such as a REST API.

options.t: The dashboard can write corrections into the store
options.why: Interactive queries are read-only.

options.t: Stores can only be queried after the application stops
options.why: Querying works while the application runs.

questions.explain: Interactive queries read local state stores, read-only. To expose the whole application's state, you add an RPC layer (for example a REST API) between instances.

questions.q: After fixing a bug, a team runs the application reset tool to reprocess everything. Which TWO things must they still handle themselves?

options.t: Resetting the input topics' offsets
options.why: The tool does this, to the beginning by default.

options.t: Deleting each instance's local state
Deleting the internal topics
options.why: The tool deletes them.

options.t: The output topics, which the tool doesn't reset
Recreating the input topics
options.why: The input topics stay; only their offsets are reset.

questions.explain: The reset tool resets input offsets and deletes internal topics; it doesn't reset output topics or delete local state, which you must do yourself.

questions.q: A team sets `topology.optimization=all` but sees no change in the topology. What is the likely cause?

options.t: Optimization only works with exactly_once_v2
options.why: Optimization is independent of the processing guarantee.

options.t: The value must be 'true', not 'all'
options.why: 'all' is a valid value.

options.t: The properties weren't also passed to StreamsBuilder.build()
Optimization needs a broker setting too
options.why: It is a Streams application setting only.

questions.explain: To apply topology optimizations, the same properties must be passed to `StreamsBuilder.build(props)` as well as set in the configuration.

questions.q: Which replication factor do a Streams application's changelog and repartition topics get by default?

options.t: Always 1
options.why: The default (-1) uses the broker's default.

options.t: The broker's default (replication.factor=-1)
Always 3
options.why: The default defers to the broker.

options.t: The same as the input topic
options.why: It comes from the replication.factor setting.

questions.explain: Streams' `replication.factor` defaults to -1, meaning the broker's default replication factor.

questions.q: Which TWO operations can mark a stream for repartitioning before a later `groupByKey()`?

options.t: selectKey
mapValues
options.why: mapValues can't change the key, so it never repartitions.

options.t: filter
options.why: filter keeps keys as they are.

options.t: map
peek
options.why: peek only looks at records.

questions.explain: `selectKey`, `map` and `flatMap` can change the key, so a grouping or join after them repartitions; `mapValues`, `filter` and `peek` don't.

questions.q: How do sliding windows in Kafka Streams differ from hopping windows?

options.t: They are aligned to record timestamps, with both bounds inclusive
They are aligned to the epoch, like tumbling and hopping windows are
options.why: Hopping and tumbling windows are epoch-aligned; sliding windows aren't.

options.t: They never overlap
options.why: Sliding windows can overlap.

options.t: They have no fixed size
options.why: That describes session windows.

questions.explain: Sliding windows are aligned to record timestamps, not the epoch, and both their bounds are inclusive. They're used for windowed aggregations and joins.

questions.q: A change data capture (CDC) feed records each insert, update and delete of a database table's rows, keyed by row ID. How should a Streams application read it to have each row's current state?

options.t: As a KStream, since each change is an event
options.why: A KStream keeps every change as an insert, not the current row.

options.t: As a windowed KStream with session windows
options.why: Sessions group activity by gaps, not by row state.

options.t: As a KTable, a changelog of the table
As a GlobalKTable only, since CDC requires one
options.why: A KTable models it; a GlobalKTable is a choice for joins, not a requirement.

questions.explain: CDC records from a database's changelog are an example of a changelog stream: read as a KTable, they give each key's latest state.

questions.q: Why does the Kafka documentation describe Kafka Streams as the simplest way to get exactly-once processing?

options.t: It never writes back to Kafka, so nothing can ever be duplicated
options.why: Streams reads from and writes to Kafka.

options.t: It disables retries everywhere
options.why: Exactly-once uses idempotence and transactions, not disabled retries.

options.t: It needs no broker support
options.why: exactly_once_v2 needs brokers 2.5 or newer.

options.t: One setting, processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2, turns it on

questions.explain: The design docs call Kafka Streams the simplest way to get exactly-once: setting `processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2` turns it on, where the plain clients need a transactional producer, offsets sent in the transaction and read_committed consumers wired by hand.

questions.q: Which artifact provides `TopologyTestDriver` for testing Kafka Streams applications?

options.t: kafka-clients
options.why: That holds the producer and consumer, not the Streams test driver.

options.t: kafka-streams-test-utils
kafka-streams-scala
options.why: That is the Scala API, deprecated in 4.3.

options.t: connect-runtime
options.why: That is Kafka Connect.

questions.explain: Kafka provides `kafka-streams-test-utils` as a separate artifact, added as a test dependency, with `TopologyTestDriver` and the test topic helpers.
